Lecture 7

Dynamics: Stone’s theorem and the free wave packet

Stone’s theorem says that the generator of every strongly continuous unitary group is self-adjoint. We prove this with vector integrals. The converse is proved for explicit diagonal and multiplication operators and sketched in general. For a free state with a rapidly decreasing transform, we compute the position variance in time.

Lecture 7, first part

Unitary groups and Stone’s theorem

7.1 Unitary groups and their generators

In Quantum Mechanics I, Thm 4.4, and in Theorem 2.2, the evolution of a system is a family of unitaries UtU_tUt​ with U0=11U_0=\IdU0​=11 and Ut+s=UtUsU_{t+s}=U_tU_sUt+s​=Ut​Us​, built from an eigenbasis of the Hamiltonian. The free energy on the line, like the position and the momentum, has no eigenbasis (Theorem 4.6). This lecture starts from the evolution instead.

We assume that the evolution is reversible and linear and that it preserves inner products. Then each UtU_tUt​ is unitary. We also assume that the law of motion does not change in time. Then evolving for a time sss and then for a time ttt is evolving for the time t+st+st+s, and evolving for no time changes nothing. This is the group law. Finally, we assume that no state jumps: for each vector ψ\psiψ, the vector UtψU_t\psiUt​ψ changes continuously with ttt.

Definition 7.1 (Unitary group). A strongly continuous unitary group on H\HilH is a family (Ut)t∈R(U_t)_{t\in\R}(Ut​)t∈R​ of unitary operators such that U0=11andUt+s=UtUsfor all real t and s,U_0=\Id\quad\text{and}\quad U_{t+s}=U_tU_s\quad\text{for all real }t\text{ and }s,U0​=11andUt+s​=Ut​Us​for all real t and s, and such that, for every ψ∈H\psi\in\Hilψ∈H, the map t↦Utψt\mapsto U_t\psit↦Ut​ψ is continuous in norm.

Since UtU−t=U0=11U_tU_{-t}=U_0=\IdUt​U−t​=U0​=11, the inverse of UtU_tUt​ is U−tU_{-t}U−t​, and since UtU_tUt​ is unitary, Ut†=U−t\adj{U_t}=U_{-t}Ut†​=U−t​. By Theorem 2.2, the evolution of the box is such a group.

Continuity in the operator norm would be a stronger requirement, and the box fails it. At the times tn=πℏ/Ent_n=\pi\hbar/E_ntn​=πℏ/En​, which tend to 000, the phase of unu_nun​ is e−iπ=−1e^{-\ii\pi}=-1e−iπ=−1, so Utnun=−unU_{t_n}u_n=-u_nUtn​​un​=−un​ and ∥Utn−11∥≥∥(Utn−11)un∥=2.\norm{U_{t_n}-\Id}\ge\norm{(U_{t_n}-\Id)u_n}=2 .∥Utn​​−11∥≥∥(Utn​​−11)un​∥=2. So the definition asks for continuity on each vector separately.

Definition 7.2 (Generator). Let (Ut)(U_t)(Ut​) be a strongly continuous unitary group. Its generator KKK has the domain D(K)\dom KD(K) of the vectors ψ\psiψ for which (Uhψ−ψ)/h(U_h\psi-\psi)/h(Uh​ψ−ψ)/h has a limit in norm as h→0h\to0h→0, and the action Kψ=ilim⁡h→0Uhψ−ψh.K\psi=\ii\lim_{h\to0}\frac{U_h\psi-\psi}h .Kψ=ih→0lim​hUh​ψ−ψ​. The general case needs the spectral theorem.

Theorem 7.5 (Every self-adjoint Hamiltonian evolvessketched). Let HHH be self-adjoint. There is a strongly continuous unitary group (e−itH/ℏ)t∈R(e^{-\ii tH/\hbar})_{t\in\R}(e−itH/ℏ)t∈R​ whose generator is H/ℏH/\hbarH/ℏ.

Proof sketch. By the spectral theorem in Hall’s multiplication form, Thm 10.10, cited, there are a measure space (X,μ)(X,\mu)(X,μ), a real measurable function ggg on XXX and a unitary U:H→L2(X,μ)U:\Hil\to\Ltwo(X,\mu)U:H→L2(X,μ) with H=U−1MgUH=U^{-1}M_gUH=U−1Mg​U. The proof of the multiplication case of Theorem 7.4 applies on XXX, with the sets where ∣g∣≤G\abs g\le G∣g∣≤G in place of [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R]. The step that makes the remainders small now needs the continuity of the measure μ\muμ, a cited tool. 

Hall, Prop. 10.14, Teschl, Thm 5.1, and Amrein, §5.1.1, give this proof with the spectral measure. By Hall’s functional calculus, Def. 10.5, used for the group in his Prop. 10.14 with the opposite sign, the group is ∫e−itλ/ℏ dEH(λ)\int e^{-\ii t\lambda/\hbar}\,\dd\pvm H(\lambda)∫e−itλ/ℏdEH​(λ). By Proposition 7.9 below, the group does not depend on the choice of UUU and ggg, and for the operators of Theorem 7.4 it is the group built there.

7.3 Stone’s theorem

By Proposition 7.3, the generator of a strongly continuous unitary group satisfies the symmetry identity. Stone’s theorem says that the generator is self-adjoint. The proof builds vectors in D(K)\dom KD(K) by averaging UtφU_t\varphiUt​φ over ttt, with the weight e−t/τe^{-t/\tau}e−t/τ. First, the average over the future lies in D(K)\dom KD(K), and this shows that K−i/τK-\ii/\tauK−i/τ maps D(K)\dom KD(K) onto H\HilH. Next, as τ→0\tau\to0τ→0 the normalised average tends to φ\varphiφ, so D(K)\dom KD(K) is dense. Then, the average over the past does the same for K+i/τK+\ii/\tauK+i/τ. Finally, the test of Proposition 6.7 gives that KKK is self-adjoint. These averages are integrals of vector functions, which we define first.

Definition 7.6 (Integral of a continuous vector function). Let f:[a,b]→Hf:[a,b]\to\Hilf:[a,b]→H be continuous in norm. A partition a=t0<t1<⋯<tN=ba=t_0<t_1<\dots<t_N=ba=t0​<t1​<⋯<tN​=b has the mesh max⁡j(tj−tj−1)\max_j(t_j-t_{j-1})maxj​(tj​−tj−1​) and the Riemann sum ∑jf(tj)(tj−tj−1)\sum_jf(t_j)(t_j-t_{j-1})∑j​f(tj​)(tj​−tj−1​). The integral ∫abf(t) dt\int_a^bf(t)\,\dd t∫ab​f(t)dt is the limit of the Riemann sums as the mesh tends to 000, and ∫baf(t) dt=−∫abf(t) dt\int_b^af(t)\,\dd t=-\int_a^bf(t)\,\dd t∫ba​f(t)dt=−∫ab​f(t)dt.

Lemma 7.7 (Vector integrals). The limit exists. It is linear in fff, it adds over adjacent intervals, and a shift of the variable does not change it: ∫abf(t+c) dt=∫a+cb+cf(s) ds\int_a^bf(t+c)\,\dd t=\int_{a+c}^{b+c}f(s)\,\dd s∫ab​f(t+c)dt=∫a+cb+c​f(s)ds. For every bounded operator AAA, A∫abf(t) dt=∫abAf(t) dtA\int_a^bf(t)\,\dd t=\int_a^bAf(t)\,\dd tA∫ab​f(t)dt=∫ab​Af(t)dt. Moreover ∥∫abf(t) dt∥≤∫ab∥f(t)∥ dt\norm{\int_a^bf(t)\,\dd t}\le\int_a^b\norm{f(t)}\,\dd t​∫ab​f(t)dt​≤∫ab​∥f(t)∥dt, and 1h∫tt+hf(s) ds⟶f(t)as h→0,\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}f(s)\,\dd s\longrightarrow f(t)\quad\text{as }h\to0 ,h1​∫tt+h​f(s)ds⟶f(t)as h→0, for ttt and t+ht+ht+h in [a,b][a,b][a,b].

Proof. As for real functions, fff is uniformly continuous on [a,b][a,b][a,b]. Given ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0, there is δ>0\delta>0δ>0 with ∥f(s)−f(t)∥<ϵ\norm{f(s)-f(t)}<\epsilon∥f(s)−f(t)∥<ϵ for ∣s−t∣<δ\abs{s-t}<\delta∣s−t∣<δ. Let a partition have mesh less than δ\deltaδ, and let a second partition contain all its points. Each interval of the first splits into intervals of the second, and the terms on them differ by values of fff at points less than δ\deltaδ apart. So the two Riemann sums differ by at most ϵ(b−a)\epsilon(b-a)ϵ(b−a). Two partitions of mesh less than δ\deltaδ have such a common refinement, so their sums differ by at most 2ϵ(b−a)2\epsilon(b-a)2ϵ(b−a). Hence the sums along partitions with mesh tending to 000 form a Cauchy sequence, and since H\HilH is complete, they converge, all to the same limit. The other claims hold for each Riemann sum, by the triangle inequality for the norm bound, and they pass to the limit since AAA and the norm are continuous. Finally, ∥1h∫tt+hf(s) ds−f(t)∥=∥1h∫tt+h(f(s)−f(t))ds∥≤max⁡∣s−t∣≤∣h∣∥f(s)−f(t)∥⟶0.\Bigl\lVert\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}f(s)\,\dd s-f(t)\Bigr\rVert =\Bigl\lVert\frac1h\int_t^{t+h}\bigl(f(s)-f(t)\bigr)\dd s\Bigr\rVert \le\max_{\abs{s-t}\le\abs h}\norm{f(s)-f(t)}\longrightarrow0 .\qedhere​h1​∫tt+h​f(s)ds−f(t)​=​h1​∫tt+h​(f(s)−f(t))ds​≤∣s−t∣≤∣h∣max​∥f(s)−f(t)∥⟶0. 

The proof of Stone’s theorem needs one integral over [0,∞)[0,\infty)[0,∞). Let f:[0,∞)→Hf:[0,\infty)\to\Hilf:[0,∞)→H be continuous, with ∥f(t)∥≤Ce−t/τ\norm{f(t)}\le Ce^{-t/\tau}∥f(t)∥≤Ce−t/τ for constants CCC and τ>0\tau>0τ>0. For T<T′T<T'T<T′, the norm bound gives ∥∫TT′f∥≤∫TT′Ce−t/τ dt≤Cτe−T/τ,\norm{\int_T^{T'}f}\le\int_T^{T'}Ce^{-t/\tau}\,\dd t\le C\tau e^{-T/\tau} ,​∫TT′​f​≤∫TT′​Ce−t/τdt≤Cτe−T/τ, so the integrals ∫0Tf\int_0^Tf∫0T​f form a Cauchy family as T→∞T\to\inftyT→∞. Their limit is ∫0∞f(t) dt\int_0^\infty f(t)\,\dd t∫0∞​f(t)dt, and it keeps the properties of Lemma 7.7.

Theorem 7.8 (Stone’s theorem). Let (Ut)(U_t)(Ut​) be a strongly continuous unitary group with the generator KKK. Then D(K)\dom KD(K) is dense, and KKK is self-adjoint. The time τ\tauτ is arbitrary, and i/τ\ii/\taui/τ has the units of KKK. In words, the resolvent of the generator is the evolution averaged over the future, with weights that fade over the time τ\tauτ. A group is fixed by its generator.

Proposition 7.9 (A group is fixed by its generator). Let (Ut)(U_t)(Ut​) and (Vt)(V_t)(Vt​) be strongly continuous unitary groups with the same generator KKK. Then Ut=VtU_t=V_tUt​=Vt​ for every ttt.

Indeed, if ψn∈D(K)\psi_n\in\dom Kψn​∈D(K) tend to χ\chiχ, then ∥Utχ−Vtχ∥≤2∥χ−ψn∥→0\norm{U_t\chi-V_t\chi}\le2\norm{\chi-\psi_n}\to0∥Ut​χ−Vt​χ∥≤2∥χ−ψn​∥→0. 

Together with the general case, the results of this section match the self-adjoint operators with the evolutions.

Theorem 7.10 (Self-adjoint operators and unitary evolutionssketched). The map H↦(e−itH/ℏ)t∈RH\mapsto(e^{-\ii tH/\hbar})_{t\in\R}H↦(e−itH/ℏ)t∈R​ is a one-to-one correspondence from the self-adjoint operators onto the strongly continuous unitary groups. Its inverse maps a group to its Hamiltonian ℏK\hbar KℏK.

Proof sketch. By Theorem 7.5, sketched, the group e−itH/ℏe^{-\ii tH/\hbar}e−itH/ℏ has the generator H/ℏH/\hbarH/ℏ, so different HHH give different groups. Let (Ut)(U_t)(Ut​) be a strongly continuous unitary group with the generator KKK. By Theorem 7.8, H=ℏKH=\hbar KH=ℏK is self-adjoint, and by Theorem 7.5 the group e−itH/ℏe^{-\ii tH/\hbar}e−itH/ℏ also has the generator KKK. By Proposition 7.9, Ut=e−itH/ℏU_t=e^{-\ii tH/\hbar}Ut​=e−itH/ℏ. 

This is the second answer to the question of why observables are self-adjoint. The Hamiltonians of unitary evolutions are exactly the self-adjoint operators. The direction from a group to a self-adjoint generator is proved in full. Only the converse needs the cited spectral theorem, and for the explicit diagonal and multiplication operators it is Theorem 7.4.

The Dirichlet momentum PDP_DPD​ of the box is symmetric, but not self-adjoint (Proposition 3.7). By Stone’s theorem, PD/ℏP_D/\hbarPD​/ℏ is the generator of no strongly continuous unitary group. So PDP_DPD​ generates no unitary evolution, and in particular no translations of the box. A translation in a box needs a rule for what happens at the walls. Lecture 9 builds the translations of the line, which the momentum PPP generates, and, for each θ\thetaθ, the translations of the box that PθP_\thetaPθ​ generates.

So the three assumptions of §7.1, a unitary evolution, a law of motion that does not change in time and no jumps, imply by Stone’s theorem that the Hamiltonian ℏK\hbar KℏK of the evolution is self-adjoint.

Lecture 7, second part

The spreading and narrowing of a free packet

7.4 The free packet

The first part proved that the Hamiltonian of a unitary evolution is self-adjoint, and that the free energy H0H_0H0​ generates the group (7.3). In this part we follow a free packet under this group. Its mean position moves with a constant velocity, its spread grows at late times, and the chirped Gaussian ψb\psi_bψb​ of §4.5 with b>0b>0b>0 first narrows.

The free evolution determines the position readings at time ttt. By Quantum Mechanics I, Prop. 4.5, the mean of an observable AAA in the state UtψU_t\psiUt​ψ is the mean of Ut†AUt\adj{U_t}AU_tUt†​AUt​ in ψ\psiψ. On the line, the position is unbounded, so we first find states that the free evolution keeps in D(Q)\dom QD(Q).

By (7.6), ΔQt/t→ΔP/m\Delta Q_t/t\to\Delta P/mΔQt​/t→ΔP/m as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞, for every such packet. At late times the spread of the positions is the spread of the velocities times ttt. By a cited theorem, Lecture 12 shows more. The probabilities of Q/tQ/tQ/t on intervals tend to those of the velocity P/mP/mP/m.

The temperature of a cold gas is measured by letting it fly. In 1988 Lett, Watts, Westbrook, Phillips, Gould and Metcalf cooled sodium atoms with laser light, switched the light off, and timed the atoms’ arrival at a probe beam below. The arrival times gave the spread of the velocities, and so the temperature: about 43 μ43\,\mu43μK, below the limit of about 240 μ240\,\mu240μK that the theory of laser cooling then predicted. At 43 μ43\,\mu43μK the velocity spread kBT/m\sqrt{k_{\mathrm B}T/m}kB​T/m​ of a sodium atom is about 0.12 0.12\,0.12m/s, so in 10 10\,10ms of flight these velocities alone displace an atom by about 1.2 1.2\,1.2mm, as an rms distance. The cloud holds many atoms and falls under gravity, so the free packet of this lecture is a model of one atom. For one free atom, (7.6) says that after a long flight its spread grows as its velocity spread times the time.

Dynamics

Evolution: the generator of every strongly continuous unitary group is self-adjoint (Theorem 7.8), and every self-adjoint HHH generates the group e−itH/ℏe^{-\ii tH/\hbar}e−itH/ℏ, proved for the explicit diagonal and multiplication operators (Theorem 7.4) and sketched in general (Theorem 7.5). The Schrödinger equation holds exactly on D(H)\dom HD(H). Observables: the Hamiltonians of unitary evolutions are the self-adjoint operators (Theorem 7.10, sketched), and the Dirichlet momentum generates no unitary group. Measurement: a free particle’s momentum density never changes. For a state with a rapidly decreasing transform, the variance of its position is quadratic in ttt (Proposition 7.12), and at late times its spread grows as ΔP t/m\Delta P\,t/mΔPt/m.

Summary

  • Unitary groups and their generators (Definitions 7.1 and 7.2): UtψU_t\psiUt​ψ is differentiable exactly on D(K)\dom KD(K), where i dUtψ/dt=KUtψ\ii\,\dd U_t\psi/\dd t=KU_t\psiidUt​ψ/dt=KUt​ψ (Proposition 7.3).
  • Evolution by an explicit Hamiltonian: diagonal operators and multiplication by a real continuous function, after a unitary, generate groups (Theorem 7.4); every self-adjoint operator does, by a sketched proof (Theorem 7.5).
  • Stone’s theorem: the generator is densely defined and self-adjoint, with the resolvents at ±i/τ\pm\ii/\tau±i/τ as Laplace integrals of the group (Theorem 7.8); a group is fixed by its generator (Proposition 7.9); self-adjoint operators and unitary evolutions correspond one to one, by a sketched proof (Theorem 7.10).
  • The free packet: if ψ~∈S(R)\fourier\psi\in\mathcal S(\R)ψ~​∈S(R), then U−tQUtψ=Qψ+tPψ/mU_{-t}QU_t\psi=Q\psi+tP\psi/mU−t​QUt​ψ=Qψ+tPψ/m, and the position variance is quadratic in ttt (Proposition 7.12); a Gaussian’s spreading time is ts=2ms2/ℏt_s=2ms^2/\hbarts​=2ms2/ℏ (Example 7.13), and a negative correlation of position and momentum makes a chirped Gaussian narrow first.

Lecture 8 evolves the harmonic oscillator, whose group returns every state, up to a common sign, after one period.

References

Other books prove some results of this lecture. Stone’s theorem with the resolvents (7.4) is Amrein, Prop. 5.1 and Cor. 5.2, with z=i/τz=\ii/\tauz=i/τ. Hall, Thm 10.15, and Teschl, Thm 5.2, prove Stone’s theorem in another way. Teta, (6.70), writes twice the real part in (7.6) as ⟨QP+PQ⟩−2⟨Q⟩⟨P⟩\langle QP+PQ\rangle-2\langle Q\rangle\langle P\rangle⟨QP+PQ⟩−2⟨Q⟩⟨P⟩.

Amrein, Hilbert Space Methods in Quantum Mechanics, §5.1.1 (p. 193), Prop. 5.1 and Cor. 5.2 (pp. 194–196). Teschl, Mathematical Methods in Quantum Mechanics, Thm 5.1 (p. 123), Thm 5.2 (p. 124). Teta, A Mathematical Primer on Quantum Mechanics, (6.70) (p. 150), (6.72) (p. 151). Quantum Mechanics I, Thm 4.4 and Prop. 4.5.
